verses.text: Now when Mordecai found out all that was done, Mordecai tore his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and a bitterly.
He came even before the king’s gate, for no one is allowed inside the king’s gate clothed with sackcloth.
In every province, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
Esther’s maidens and her eunuchs came and told her this, and the queen was exceedingly grieved. She sent clothing to Mordecai, to replace his sackcloth; but he didn’t receive it.
Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs, whom he had appointed to attend her, and commanded him to go to Mordecai, to find out what this was, and why it was.
So Hathach went out to Mordecai, to city square which was before the king’s gate.
Mordecai told him of all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king’s treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.

He also gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given out in Shushan to destroy them, to show it to Esther, and to declare it to her, and to urge her to go in to the king, to make supplication to him, and to make request before him, for her people.
Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and gave him a message to Mordecai:

“All the king’s servants, and the people of the king’s provinces, know, that whoever, whether man or woman, comes to the king into the inner court without being called, there is one law for him, that he be put to death, except those to whom the king might hold out the golden scepter, that he may live. I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days.”
They told to Mordecai Esther’s words.
Then Mordecai asked them return answer to Esther, “Don’t think to yourself that you will escape in the king’s house any more than all the Jews.

For if you remain silent now, then relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”
Then Esther asked them to answer Mordecai,

“Go, gather together all the Jews who are present in Shushan, and fast for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day. I and my maidens will also fast the same way. Then I will go in to the king, which is against the law; and if I perish, I perish.”
So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.

footnotes.content: Mordecai's grief is so deep it breaks him open in the street. That sackcloth and ash—it's not for show. When our people are condemned to death, we feel it in our whole body, and sometimes the truest prayer is just to grieve out loud where everyone can see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's gate is a boundary—no sackcloth allowed inside. Mordecai stops at the threshold but doesn't turn back; he stays where the king can see him, a silent witness to what needs to be answered. Sometimes faithfulness is just staying put and letting others see what grief looks like.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the heart of the kingdom to every province, one sorrow spreads through God's people. That unity in mourning is itself a form of witness—the whole people bound together in the same fear, fasting, and weeping. In our weakness, we learn we are not alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther's first move is to comfort Mordecai, to dress him in something better. But he refuses—he won't be clothed in anything less than truth right now. Sometimes love means letting someone stay in their sorrow until the sorrow is answered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther sends Hathach to find out what's wrong. She doesn't stay in her palace and guess—she reaches out, asking real questions, ready to listen. That willingness to be disturbed and to ask is where rescue begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hathach crosses the palace threshold to meet Mordecai in the city square. He carries the question from inside the walls to outside, from the queen to the grieving man. Faithful messengers go where love sends them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai lays it all out—every detail of Haman's plot and the price tag on destruction. He holds nothing back from his messenger. There's no point in hiding the truth from someone who might help; we have to name the threat clearly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The actual decree—written, official, deadly. Mordecai sends proof so Esther will know this isn't rumor or fear; it's law. Then he asks her to go to the king, to plead and petition for her own people. He's asking her to risk everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hathach carries the weight of sorrow from the street back into the palace. He delivers Mordecai's words to Esther exactly. A faithful messenger doesn't soften the message or add his own opinion; he brings the truth as he heard it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther answers Hathach with a message back to Mordecai. She doesn't ignore what she's heard, and she doesn't panic. She responds—which means she's thinking, she's weighing what's being asked of her.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The law of the Persian court is absolute: enter the king's inner chamber unbidden and you die, unless he holds out his scepter. Esther hasn't been called in thirty days. She's telling Mordecai the truth: I cannot just walk in without being summoned. To approach would be to face death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai receives Esther's words—her fear, her caution, her explanation of what the law forbids. He hears that she understands the cost. But he doesn't let the message settle there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai cuts through Esther's fear with a hard question: Do you think your rank will save you? No. You're Jewish too. You can't hide from this in a palace—safety lies somewhere else, not in silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the hinge of the story: 'Who knows if you haven't come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' Mordecai doesn't name God, but he knows deliverance will come—from somewhere, somehow. And he's asking Esther: What if your place here, right now, is the answer? What if this is why you were chosen queen?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esther answers Mordecai—not with refusal, but with a plan. She's decided. Now she's telling him what she needs from her people: a fast, three days, night and day, so we can align ourselves with what needs to happen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then she says it: 'If I perish, I perish.' Those five words are everything—surrender, courage, love for her people, and trust in something she cannot see. She will break the law. She will approach the king unbidden. She knows it might cost her life, and she's chosen to do it anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mordecai leaves. He doesn't second-guess what Esther has decided. He simply does what she commanded—he carries her word to the people, he calls the fast, he obeys. Sometimes the bravest thing is to trust another person's courage and get out of the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
